easy.heading: Warming Up With a Few Doubles
easy.body:
I started today with a fresh cup of coffee and the easy grid, which felt like a nice gentle way to wake up the brain. The first thing that caught my eye were the empty spots at (0,0) and (2,2). In these puzzles, empty usually means a value of zero, so I knew those cells would be the low ends of whatever dominoes I placed there. I quickly looked for my higher values and saw the sum of 6 required at (0,4) and (0,5). Looking at my tray, the [3,3] domino was the perfect fit to hit that target exactly.

Next, I moved over to the equals region involving (1,3), (1,4), and (2,3). This one is a bit of a chain. Since (1,3) and (1,4) are paired up as a single domino, I decided to try the [4,4] there. That meant the cell at (2,3) also had to be a 4 to satisfy the equals constraint. This left me with a few spots for the [1,1] and [6,1] dominoes. I placed the [6,1] so that the 6 landed on the greater than 3 constraint at (1,2), which felt like the last piece of the puzzle falling into place. It was a satisfying start to the morning!
easy.solution_logic: Matches [4,4] to equals, [3,3] to sum 6, and [6,1] to the greater than 3 cell.

medium.heading: Stepping Up the Challenge with Double Digits
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today was definitely a step up, mostly because of that big sum of 12 across the top row from (0,0) to (0,3). I spent a few minutes hovering my mouse over the tray, trying to see which combination of my dominoes like [6,2] and [5,3] could reach 12 without blocking the rest of the board. I eventually realized that the [6,2] and [1,4] dominoes worked best when split across those four cells. The 6 and 4 provided the bulk of the value I needed.

The real trick to this one was the less than 2 constraint at (2,1) and (2,2). With the sum needing to stay so low, I knew I had to use my [0,0] domino there. Placing that double zero really cleared things up for the bottom of the grid. It allowed me to use the [3,3] for the greater than 5 constraint at (3,2) and (3,3). Once those anchors were in, I just had to make sure the remaining equals regions at (1,3) and (2,3) matched up with the leftover values from my [4,3] and [5,3] dominoes.
medium.solution_logic: Uses [0,0] for the less than 2 area and strategically places [6,2] and [1,4] for the sum of 12.

hard.heading: Navigating the Twists of the Hardest Grid
hard.body:
Rodolfo Kurchan really outdid himself with the hard grid today! The complexity of the equals constraints connecting cells like (2,0), (2,1), (3,0), and (4,0) meant that one wrong move at the start would ruin everything later. I initially struggled with the bottom row, but then I spotted the sum of 0 at (3,3) and (3,4). That is a very specific clue because it forces you to use a domino with a zero in it. I used that as my anchor point and worked outward.

The breakthrough happened when I looked at the greater than 4 constraints at (3,5), (4,1), and (5,0). I had to save my [5,4] and [3,5] dominoes specifically for those spots. I placed the [3,5] at (2,5) and (3,5), which satisfied the greater than constraint at the bottom while helping with the sum of 2 up at (2,4) and (2,5). It was like a giant domino effect, literally! Once those high values were locked in, the equals regions for (4,2), (4,3), (5,2), and (5,3) became much easier to balance using the [4,3] and [2,2] dominoes. This one took me two cups of coffee to finish, but the feeling of completing that perfectly balanced grid was worth it.
hard.solution_logic: Focuses on the sum 0 constraint as a starting point and uses high-value dominoes like [3,5] and [5,4] for the greater than 4 spots.

explanation.tips: My best advice for Pips is to always look for the most restrictive constraints first, like a sum of 0 or a very high sum like 12. These usually only have one or two possible domino combinations. Also, keep an eye on your tray and identify your unique dominoes, like double zeros or high-value doubles, because they usually have a very specific home on the board. If you find yourself stuck, try removing the last two dominoes you placed; often a small mistake in an equals region can ripple across the whole grid.
explanation.learned: Today I learned just how much a single 0 can change the layout of a puzzle. In the hard grid, that sum of 0 was the key to the entire right side of the board. It is also interesting to see how the editor, Ian Livengood, uses equals constraints to link different columns together, forcing you to think about the grid as a whole rather than just focusing on one small corner at a time. I am definitely going to look for those linking regions first in tomorrow's puzzle.

faqs.question: How do you solve the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: To solve Pips, you must place all the dominoes from your tray onto the grid so that they satisfy every mathematical constraint, such as sums, equals, and greater than or less than signs.

faqs.question: What does the empty cell mean in a Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: An empty cell in a Pips puzzle region usually indicates that the cell must contain zero pips. This often requires you to use a domino that has a 0 on one or both sides.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes can only be placed horizontally or vertically. Each domino covers two adjacent cells on the grid.

faqs.question: What does the equals sign between regions mean?
faqs.answer: The equals sign means that the total number of pips in one region must be exactly the same as the total number of pips in the connected region.

faqs.question: Is there only one solution to the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, every daily NYT Pips puzzle is designed to have one unique solution that satisfies all the given constraints and uses all the provided dominoes.

faqs.question: How do sum constraints work in Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum constraint gives you a target number. The total number of pips in all the cells within that specific colored region must add up to that target number.
